definition: Disruptive means causing disruption; disturbing the normal course or flow of something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disruptive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disruptive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The month-long roadwork on Main Street was so disruptive that the bus company had to reroute six lines and print entirely new schedules.
A distracting noise pulls your attention away for a moment, while a disruptive one actually breaks the flow of what a group is doing.
A disruptive event interrupts the normal routine, but a chaotic one destroys order completely, leaving no routine at all.

Disturbing means interfering with someone's peace, order, or concentration, like a disturbing racket from the apartment upstairs; in everyday use it also means troubling. Disruptive is more concrete: it breaks the normal flow of an activity, knocking a class, meeting, or performance off course.

Disorderly means breaking the normal order of things, as in disorderly conduct or a disorderly queue; it describes behavior or a state that ignores the rules of order. Disruptive aims at an ongoing activity: a disruptive thing interrupts what a group is doing.

Obstructive means getting in the way of progress, often deliberately, the way an obstructive official slows every request; it blocks movement toward a goal. Disruptive breaks the flow of what is already happening: a disruptive noise shatters a meeting's rhythm rather than blocking its goal.

Neutral / everyday and business
Disruptive commonly appears in 'disruptive behavior' and 'disruptive noise,' and in business writing 'disruptive technology' can even carry a positive spin of shaking up an industry.
Keep it distinct from divisive: disruptive means interrupting the normal flow or functioning of something, while divisive means causing people to take opposing sides.

The newsroom had run on the same rhythm for twenty years: reporters wrote until six, editors marked pages until eight, and the presses started at nine.
Then the building's owners began replacing the elevators, and the freight car that carried each evening's printing plates went out of service.
The change proved far more disruptive than anyone had predicted.
Plates had to be hand-carried down four flights of stairs, editors stopped early to allow for the climb, and the presses sat waiting, sometimes forty minutes past their start time.
Nothing was damaged and nobody was hurt; the machines simply could not keep their old rhythm, and for six weeks the paper reached porches an hour late.
